title: How to Change an HVAC Filter, Step by Step
h1: How to Change an HVAC Filter: A Simple Step-by-Step
description: Changing an HVAC filter takes a few minutes. Learn where to find it, how to pick the right size and which way the airflow arrow should point in your home.
quick_answer: To change an HVAC filter, turn the system off, find the filter at a return grille or the furnace, note the size printed on the frame, slide the old one out and insert a new filter with the airflow arrow pointing toward the furnace or air handler. Close the cover, turn the system back on, and write the date on the new filter.
body:
What do you need before you start?

Changing a filter is one of the easiest bits of home maintenance you can do. All you need is:

  • A new filter in the exact size of your current one
  • A screwdriver if your return grille is held by screws
  • A marker to write the date on the frame
  • A trash bag for the old filter, especially if it's very dusty
  • A step stool if the return grille is in the ceiling

Where is the HVAC filter in your home?

Most Southern California homes don't have basements, so the filter is usually in one of these spots:

  • Return grille in a hallway ceiling or wall. The large grille, often the biggest vent in the house, opens on hinges or clips.
  • Furnace in a hall closet. Look for a slot on the side or bottom of the furnace cabinet.
  • Furnace in the garage. Same as the closet setup, often with a slot near the base.
  • Air handler in the attic. Some homes have the filter right at the unit, which is easy to forget.

Some homes have more than one return and more than one filter. Check every large grille.

How do you change the filter step by step?

  1. Turn the system off at the thermostat. This keeps the blower from pulling dust in while the filter is out.
  2. Open the grille or filter door. Unlatch the clips or remove the screws.
  3. Note the size and arrow direction. The size, such as 20x25x1, is printed on the frame. Notice which way the arrow points.
  4. Slide out the old filter gently. Keep it level so dust doesn't fall off. Put it straight into a bag.
  5. Wipe the slot or grille. A damp cloth or vacuum removes loose dust.
  6. Insert the new filter. The airflow arrow should point toward the furnace or air handler, which means into the ductwork at a return grille.
  7. Close the grille or door. Make sure it's latched snugly with no gaps.
  8. Write the date on the frame and turn the system back on.

How do you choose the right replacement filter?

Start with the exact size. A filter that's too small leaves gaps, and air will take the path of least resistance around it. Then choose the type:

  • Fiberglass filters are inexpensive and protect the equipment, but they catch very little fine dust.
  • Pleated filters catch more dust, pollen and pet dander, and are a good choice for most homes.
  • Higher MERV filters catch smaller particles but can restrict airflow on some systems. Ask a technician if your system can handle one.
  • Media filters are four or five inches thick and fit in a special cabinet. They last longer and filter well.

Our indoor air quality service can help you pick the right filter, or install a media cabinet if you want better filtration.

How often should you change it?

Check the filter every month. Most one-inch pleated filters need replacing every one to three months. Homes with pets, allergies, construction dust or wildfire smoke need more frequent changes. Thick media filters often last six months or more.

If the filter looks gray and you can't see light through it, it's time.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Installing the filter backward, against the airflow arrow
  • Using the wrong size and leaving gaps
  • Running the system with no filter while you go to the store
  • Forgetting a second return or the attic air handler filter
  • Trying to wash a disposable filter

If you change the filter and still notice weak airflow, odd smells or ice on the refrigerant lines, there may be another issue in the system that a technician should look at.

Is there anything special about attic filters?

If your filter is at an air handler in the attic, take extra care. Step only on the framing or a walkway, never on the drywall between joists, and bring a flashlight. Attics get very hot during inland summers, so change the filter in the morning when it's cooler.

Because attic filters are out of sight, they're the ones most often forgotten. Setting a monthly phone reminder helps, or ask a technician whether a return grille filter location inside the house would be practical for your system.
faqs: Which way should the arrow on an HVAC filter point?
The arrow should point in the direction the air flows, toward the furnace or air handler. At a return grille in the ceiling or wall, that means pointing into the duct, away from the room.
Can I run my HVAC without a filter for a short time?
It's best not to. Even a short time without a filter lets dust go straight onto the blower and coil. Keep a spare filter on hand so you never have to.
What if I can't find my filter size?
Measure the length, width and thickness of the slot or old filter. Filters are labeled by nominal size, which may be slightly larger than the actual measurement, so compare with sizes sold in stores.
Are washable filters a good idea?
They can work if you clean them often and let them dry completely before reinstalling. Many washable filters catch less fine dust than good pleated disposable filters.
Where Is the HVAC Filter Located in Your Home?

Most HVAC filters are in one of two places: behind a return air grille in a ceiling or wall, or in a slot or cabinet right at the furnace or air handler. In Southern California homes, check the hallway ceiling first, then the garage, a hall closet or the attic where the equipment sits.
Which Way Does the Air Filter Go in Your HVAC System?

The arrow on the filter frame should point in the direction the air moves: toward the furnace or air handler and away from the room. At a ceiling return grille, the arrow points up. At a wall grille, it points into the wall. At the furnace, it points toward the blower.
How Do You Measure and Find the Right HVAC Filter Size?

Check the size printed on the edge of your current filter, listed as length by width by depth in inches. If there's no label, measure the filter or the filter slot with a tape measure. Filters are sold by a rounded nominal size, so the actual size is usually slightly smaller. The filter should fit snugly with no gaps.
